## Recap: From Hadoop to Spark

Module 3 ended with MapReduce's biggest weakness: **every job writes its intermediate results to
disk**, even between steps of the same pipeline. For a job that only runs once, that's fine. For
anything iterative — trying 100 variations of a machine-learning model, or chaining ten
transformations together — writing to disk every single step is slow.

**Apache Spark** was built to fix exactly this.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** Just re-anchor: MapReduce's map→shuffle→reduce→disk cycle from Module 3 is the
thing Spark is reacting against. Don't re-teach MapReduce, just point at the pain point.
:::

---

## What Is Apache Spark?

**Apache Spark** is a distributed data-processing engine — the successor to Hadoop MapReduce for
most large-scale data work today.

- **Key idea:** keep intermediate data **in memory** across steps of a pipeline, instead of
  writing every step to disk the way MapReduce does.
- Result: **10–100× faster** for workloads that reuse the same data across multiple steps
  (iterative algorithms, interactive queries, multi-stage pipelines).
- Written in Scala, but has full APIs in Python (**PySpark** — what we use), Java, R, and SQL.
- Beyond the batch DataFrame work this course focuses on, Spark also has Spark SQL (write actual
  SQL queries against a DataFrame), Structured Streaming (process data as it arrives, not just in
  batches), and MLlib (distributed machine learning) — all part of the same engine, not separate
  tools. We only use the batch/DataFrame piece this semester.
- **In our classroom cluster**, Spark jobs happen to read from HDFS and get scheduled by YARN,
  both from Module 3 — but that's a choice about *our* setup, not a requirement of Spark itself.
  Spark can just as easily read from S3, local files, a database, or a Kafka stream; it isn't
  tied to HDFS the way MapReduce, in practice, always was.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Emphasize continuity, not replacement: HDFS and YARN don't go away in our
setup. Spark is a new way to *compute*, sitting on the same storage and scheduling layer already
taught — but say explicitly that this is *our* classroom's configuration, not a general Spark
requirement (Final Q17 tests this distinction directly: Spark is not tied to HDFS). The SQL/
streaming/MLlib bullet is Quiz 5 Q9's multi-select — keep it to one sentence each, this course
never touches any of the three.
:::

---

## Why Spark Improves on MapReduce

Picture a pipeline with three steps: filter, then group, then sort.

- **MapReduce:** step 1 writes its full output to disk. Step 2 reads it back from disk, computes,
  writes its output to disk. Step 3 does the same. Three disk round-trips for one pipeline.
- **Spark:** step 1's output stays in memory. Step 2 reads it from memory, computes, keeps its
  result in memory. Step 3 does the same. Disk is only touched if you explicitly ask Spark to
  save something, or if data is too big to fit in memory.

::: {.callout-important}
This matters most for **iterative** workloads — anything that reuses the same data repeatedly,
like training a machine-learning model over many passes. A single MapReduce-style batch job that
runs once and finishes isn't dramatically slower in MapReduce; it's *repeated* work over the same
data where Spark's in-memory model wins big.
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** This is Quiz 5's Q1 almost verbatim — spend real time here. The wrong-but-
tempting answer is "Spark just has better algorithms"; the right answer is specifically about
avoiding repeated disk I/O across steps.
:::

---

## RDDs vs. DataFrames

Spark actually has two ways to represent distributed data. You need to know both exist, even
though we will work almost entirely with the second one.

| | **RDD** (Resilient Distributed Dataset) | **DataFrame** |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | A low-level, distributed collection of *arbitrary* Python objects | A distributed table — named columns, with a schema |
| Structure | None enforced — Spark doesn't know what's inside | Spark knows every column's name and type |
| Optimization | None — you write exactly what runs | Spark's optimizer can rewrite your query to run faster |
| Feels like | A distributed Python list | A distributed spreadsheet |

- RDDs came first (Spark's original data structure) and are still there underneath everything.
- DataFrames were added later, and are what virtually everyone uses for tabular data today —
  including everything in this course, the labs, and the capstone.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Think about it
If Spark doesn't know what's *inside* an RDD, what can't it do that it *can* do with a
DataFrame? (Hint: think about what "optimizing a query" requires knowing about the data first.)
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 5 min.** This slide exists specifically because Quiz 5's Q2 asks students to
distinguish RDD from DataFrame directly — don't let this be a one-line footnote. The answer to
the callout: without column names/types, Spark can't reorder operations, push filters down, or
pick an efficient join strategy — it just has to run your code as literally written.
:::

---

## Spark Architecture

```
┌──────────────────────────────────┐
│         Driver Program           │  ← your Python script
│  SparkContext / SparkSession     │
└──────────────┬───────────────────┘
               │ task distribution
    ┌──────────┼──────────┐
┌───▼───┐  ┌──▼────┐  ┌──▼────┐
│Exec 1 │  │Exec 2 │  │Exec 3 │  ← workers (run tasks)
└───────┘  └───────┘  └───────┘
    ↑           ↑          ↑
    └───────────┴──────────┘
         Cluster Manager
              (YARN)
```

- **Driver:** coordinates the whole computation — your code runs here, and it decides what work
  to hand out. Plays the same role Module 3's **ApplicationMaster** played for a MapReduce job:
  one coordinator, dispatched for this one application.
- **Executor:** a worker process that actually runs tasks and holds a slice of the data in
  memory — the same role Module 3's **NodeManager**-run tasks played, just for Spark tasks instead
  of Map/Reduce tasks.
- **Cluster manager:** allocates machines/resources to your job — in our classroom cluster,
  that's **YARN**, the exact same resource manager Module 3 used for MapReduce jobs. Spark doesn't
  bring its own scheduler here; it asks YARN for workers, the same way a MapReduce job did.

::: {.callout-note}
## Diagram to add later (Excalidraw / pyxcd / draw.io)
A "Driver" box at the top (drawn like a small laptop/script icon, since it's literally "your
Python code"), with a downward arrow labeled "task distribution" fanning out to three "Executor"
icons (worker/gear icons, each shown holding a small stack of data-block icons to represent

upward arrows from each Executor back into it, visually matching Module 3's YARN diagram's
ResourceManager/NodeManager icon style so students recognize it as the same underlying system.
Caption: "Same YARN as Module 3 — just handing out Spark tasks instead of Map/Reduce tasks."
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** The payoff line: "you already learned what YARN does in Module 3 — Spark just
hands YARN a different kind of job to schedule." Don't re-explain YARN from scratch.
:::

## SparkSession — Your Entry Point

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

# Create (or reuse) a SparkSession
spark = SparkSession.builder \
    .appName("MyFirstSparkJob") \
    .getOrCreate()

print(spark.version)
```

- Every PySpark program starts by creating (or reusing) exactly **one** `SparkSession`.
- `.getOrCreate()` — if a session already exists, reuse it; otherwise, create a new one.
- **In our classroom setup:** every `%%spark` notebook cell (via `sparkmagic`, from Lab 6) already
  has a `spark` object ready to use — you skip the `SparkSession.builder` step entirely in Labs 7
  and 8 and the capstone. You'll still write it by hand for Checkpoint 4, since checkpoints are
  graded as standalone code.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** Flag the discrepancy explicitly: checkpoints want the full `SparkSession.builder...`
line (Quiz 5 Q3 tests this exact syntax); the labs' `%%spark` cells already have `spark` built for
you. Both are correct, in their own context — this is not a contradiction.
:::

## Creating and Inspecting a DataFrame

```python
data = [
    ("Alice", "Engineering", 95000),
    ("Bob",   "Marketing",   62000),
]
columns = ["name", "department", "salary"]

df = spark.createDataFrame(data, columns)

df.printSchema()   # show column names and inferred types
df.show()           # print the rows
```

- `printSchema()` shows you the column names and the types Spark inferred for each.
- `show()` prints rows to the screen — and, importantly, it's the first thing on this slide that
  actually **runs** anything (more on why that distinction matters in a few slides).
- You can also read a DataFrame straight from a file — covered in full next session.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** This mirrors Lab 7 Task 1 almost exactly — flag that connection so students
recognize the lab as "the same two commands you just saw, applied to your own data."
:::

---

## DataFrames Are Immutable

**Every PySpark DataFrame, once created, never changes.** Every operation returns a **brand-new**
DataFrame — the original is always left untouched.

```python
filtered = df.filter(df["salary"] > 70000)

# df itself is completely unchanged here — still has all rows
# filtered is a NEW DataFrame with only the matching rows
```

::: {.callout-important}
This trips up almost everyone coming from pandas or spreadsheets, where you're used to modifying
data in place. In PySpark, if you don't **assign the result** of an operation to a variable, the
result is thrown away and nothing changes. `df.filter(...)` on its own line, with no `=`, does
nothing useful.
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** Quiz 5's Q6 asks this directly (true/false, "does filter() modify df in
place?"). Say the rule out loud, plainly, more than once — it's one of the most-missed ideas in
this whole module.
:::

---

## Lazy Evaluation — The Core Idea

```python
# These lines define a PLAN — nothing runs yet
filtered   = df.filter(df["salary"] > 70000)
selected   = filtered.select("name", "salary")
sorted_df  = selected.orderBy("salary", ascending=False)

# THIS triggers computation — Spark executes the whole plan at once
sorted_df.show()
```

- Nothing above `sorted_df.show()` actually touches the data. Spark just **records** each step as
  part of a plan — this is called **lazy evaluation**.
- That recorded plan has a name: a **DAG** (Directed Acyclic Graph) — a chain of steps that only
  ever flows forward, never loops back on itself. Each transformation you chain adds one more
  step to the DAG; nothing runs until an action triggers the whole thing at once.
- Only when you call an action (`show()`, `count()`, ...) does Spark look at the *entire* DAG you
  built, optimize it, and run it all at once.
- Why bother? Because seeing the whole plan first lets Spark skip unnecessary work — for example,
  if you `filter()` then `select()` two columns, Spark can avoid ever reading the columns you
  didn't ask for.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 5 min.** Quiz 5's Q8 tests this definition directly. The "why bother" bullet is the
part students usually skip — don't let this be just "Spark waits to run things," make sure they
leave with *why* waiting is useful. The DAG bullet is here specifically because Lab 7 Task 2 asks
"What is a DAG in Spark? When does Spark build it and when does it execute it?" as a graded
question — without this bullet, that question would be untaught.
:::

---

## Transformations vs. Actions

| Transformations (lazy — build the plan) | Actions (trigger execution) |
|---|---|
| `filter()` | `show()` |
| `select()` | `count()` |
| `groupBy()` | `collect()` |
| `orderBy()` | `write.csv()` |
| `withColumn()` | `first()` |
| `join()` | `take(n)` |

::: {.callout-tip}
If a line of PySpark code **returns a DataFrame**, it's a transformation. If it **returns data or
writes a file**, it's an action.
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** This table is the single most quiz-relevant slide in the session — Quiz 5 Q10
and Quiz 6 Q2 both hinge on this exact distinction. Have students apply the rule-of-thumb callout
to two or three examples out loud before moving on.
:::

## Recap: Transformations, Actions, Laziness

Three ideas from Monday, quickly:

- **Transformations** (`filter`, `select`, ...) build a plan but don't run anything.
- **Actions** (`show`, `count`, ...) trigger Spark to actually execute that plan.
- **DataFrames are immutable** — every transformation returns a *new* DataFrame; you must assign
  the result or it's discarded.

Today: turning real files into DataFrames, and the two most common transformations you'll use on
almost every dataset — filtering rows and selecting columns.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** Fast recap only — the point is to have the vocabulary ready, not re-teach it.
:::

---

## Loading Data into Spark

```python
# CSV with a header row
df = spark.read.csv("path/to/file.csv", header=True, inferSchema=True)

# TSV (tab-separated) with no header
df = spark.read.csv("path/to/file.tsv", sep="\t", header=False, inferSchema=True)

# JSON
df = spark.read.json("path/to/file.json")

# From HDFS — always your own username, never a shared placeholder
df = spark.read.csv("hdfs:///user/<your-username>/data.csv", header=True, inferSchema=True)
```

- `header=True` tells Spark the first row is column names, not data.
- `inferSchema=True` tells Spark to scan the file and guess each column's type (integer, string,
  double, ...) rather than treating every value as text.
- Reading `hdfs://...` paths works exactly the same as reading a local path — Spark doesn't care
  where the file lives, as long as it can reach it.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Quiz 5 Q4 tests this exact syntax verbatim (`spark.read.csv(..., header=True,
inferSchema=True)`) — make sure students see and can reproduce it, not just recognize it.
:::

---

## A Word on Schemas

- Without `inferSchema=True`, Spark treats **every** column as a string — even columns that are
  clearly numbers. Filtering `df["salary"] > 70000` on a string column silently does the wrong
  thing (string comparison, not numeric).
- `inferSchema=True` costs a little extra time (Spark has to scan the file first), but for
  anything you'll filter or aggregate numerically, it's worth it.
- `df.printSchema()` is your first move on *any* new dataset — confirm the types are what you
  expect before writing a single transformation.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Think about it
You load a CSV and `printSchema()` shows a `price` column typed as `string`, not `double`. What's
the most likely cause — and what's the first thing you'd check in the raw file?
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** The intended answer to the callout: either `inferSchema` was left off, or the
column has some non-numeric values mixed in (e.g. `"N/A"`) that forced Spark to fall back to
string for the whole column.
:::

## Filtering Rows

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import col

# Filter rows — both forms below are equivalent
high_earners = df.filter(df["salary"] > 70000)
high_earners = df.filter(col("salary") > 70000)

# You can also pass a filter as a plain SQL-style string
high_earners = df.filter("salary > 70000")

# .where() is just another name for the same thing
high_earners = df.where(df["salary"] > 70000)
```

- `df["salary"]` and `col("salary")` are two ways of referring to the same column — use whichever
  reads more clearly in context.
- `filter()` and `where()` are exact synonyms — pick one and be consistent.
- Remember: this **returns a new DataFrame**. `high_earners` is new; `df` still has every row.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Quiz 6 Q10 lists several of these forms as "select all that apply" — students
need to recognize *all* of them as valid, not just the one they memorize.
:::

---

## Selecting and Renaming Columns

```python
# Select specific columns
result = df.select("name", "department", "salary")

# Add a new computed column
df = df.withColumn("salary_k", col("salary") / 1000)

# Rename a column
df = df.withColumnRenamed("salary", "annual_salary")
```

- `select()` keeps only the columns you name, in the order you name them, dropping the rest.
- `withColumn(name, expression)` adds a new column computed from existing ones — or overwrites an
  existing column if you reuse its name.
- `withColumnRenamed(old, new)` changes a column's name without touching its values.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Quiz 5 Q7 tests `select()` directly. Point out the parallel with the earlier
filter-forms slide: these are all just "transformation in, new DataFrame out," same pattern every
time.
:::

---

## Adding a Computed Column

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import col

# Wrong — this is pandas syntax, and it doesn't work in Spark
df["new_col"] = df["col1"] * 2

# Right — Spark syntax
df = df.withColumn("new_col", col("col1") * 2)
```

The pandas-style assignment on the first line above doesn't raise an error that's obviously about
this mistake — it just fails, because PySpark DataFrames don't support item assignment the way
pandas DataFrames do. `withColumn` is the only correct way to add or replace a column.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** This is worth its own slide (not folded into "common mistakes") because it's
the single most common first bug students hit in Lab 7 — the error message is unhelpful, so
seeing the correct pattern *before* hitting the bug saves real debugging time.
:::

---

## Avoiding Common PySpark Mistakes

```python
# ❌ Wrong — using a Python list comprehension on a Spark DataFrame
result = [row for row in df if row["salary"] > 70000]  # doesn't use Spark at all

# ✅ Right — use Spark's own filter
result = df.filter(col("salary") > 70000)

# ❌ Wrong — forgetting that filter() doesn't modify df in place
df.filter(col("salary") > 70000)   # result thrown away — df is unchanged
high_earners = df.filter(col("salary") > 70000)  # correct — result is captured
```

- A Python `for` loop over a DataFrame technically works, but it pulls everything to a single
  machine and processes it one row at a time in plain Python — throwing away everything Spark is
  for.
- The second mistake is the immutability rule from Session 1, showing up again in real code — if
  your DataFrame "isn't changing," check whether you forgot to assign the result.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 5 min.** Both of these are genuinely common — if time is short, prioritize the second
one, since it's the more frequent real bug in student code across every lab this module.
:::

---

## Worked Example: Filter → Select

Given a DataFrame `employees` with columns `name`, `department`, `salary`:

```python
# Goal: names and salaries of everyone in Marketing earning over $60,000

marketing_high_earners = employees \
    .filter(col("department") == "Marketing") \
    .filter(col("salary") > 60000) \
    .select("name", "salary")

marketing_high_earners.show()
```

- Multiple `.filter()` calls chain naturally — each one narrows the DataFrame further.
- Order between the two filters here doesn't change the result, but `select()` **must** come
  after both filters — once you `select()` away a column, you can no longer filter on it.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** This example deliberately uses a different scenario from Checkpoint 4's own
`movies.csv` example (below) so it doesn't spoil the checkpoint — but it's the exact same
filter→select shape students are about to be graded on.
:::

## GroupBy and Aggregation

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import avg, count, round as spark_round, desc

# Average salary and headcount by department
df.groupBy("department") \
  .agg(
      spark_round(avg("salary"), 2).alias("avg_salary"),
      count("name").alias("num_employees")
  ) \
  .orderBy(desc("avg_salary")) \
  .show()
```

- `groupBy("column")` — a transformation; it doesn't compute anything on its own, it just says
  "gather rows into groups by this column's value."
- `.agg(...)` — applies one or more aggregation functions (`avg`, `count`, `sum`, ...) to each
  group, producing one output row per group.
- `.alias("name")` — renames the resulting column to something readable.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Quiz 6 Q1 and Q5 both test reading/predicting `groupBy().agg()` /
`groupBy().sum()` output directly — walk through what the *output shape* looks like (one row per
distinct group value), not just the syntax.
:::

---

## Aggregation Functions Reference

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import (
    avg, count, sum as spark_sum, min, max, countDistinct
)

df.groupBy("category").agg(
    count("*").alias("total_rows"),
    avg("price").alias("avg_price"),
    spark_sum("revenue").alias("total_revenue"),
    min("price").alias("cheapest"),
    max("price").alias("most_expensive")
)
```

| Function | What it computes |
|---|---|
| `count()` | Number of rows (per group, or `count("*")` for all rows) |
| `avg()` | Mean of a numeric column |
| `sum()` | Total of a numeric column — note the `as spark_sum` import alias, since `sum` is also a Python built-in |
| `min()` / `max()` | Smallest / largest value |
| `countDistinct()` | Number of *unique* values |

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** The `sum as spark_sum` import quirk is worth calling out explicitly — students
who skip it and just write `sum(...)` get confusing errors from Python's built-in `sum()`
shadowing the Spark one.
:::

---

## `orderBy` and the Top-N Pattern

```python
# The "top N by some metric" pattern — you'll use this constantly
top_5 = df.groupBy("department") \
          .agg(spark_round(avg("salary"), 2).alias("avg_salary")) \
          .orderBy("avg_salary", ascending=False) \
          .limit(5)

top_5.show()
```

- `orderBy(column, ascending=False)` sorts descending; `ascending=True` (or omitting it) sorts
  ascending.
- `.limit(n)` keeps only the first `n` rows after sorting.
- `.show(n)` — a shortcut that sorts-then-limits-then-prints in one call, when you don't need the
  limited DataFrame for anything else afterward.

::: {.callout-tip}
This exact pattern — `groupBy → agg → orderBy → limit/show(n)` — is precisely what Checkpoint 5
asks you to do, and it's the core of Lab 8's "top 10 highest-rated movies" task.
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Quiz 6 Q4 tests `orderBy(..., ascending=False)` syntax directly. Flag the
Checkpoint 5 connection out loud — this slide is deliberately the most directly test-relevant one
in the session.
:::

## Actions, Revisited: The Risk of `collect()`

Session 1 introduced actions as "the things that trigger execution." One of them deserves a
warning of its own.

```python
# ⚠️ Dangerous on a large DataFrame
all_rows = df.collect()   # pulls EVERY row to the driver machine, as a Python list

# ✅ Safer — limit first
sample = df.limit(100).collect()
```

- `collect()` brings **all** matching rows back to the driver program, as ordinary Python
  objects — not distributed anymore.
- If the DataFrame is large, this can **crash the driver** — the driver has one machine's worth of
  memory, not the whole cluster's.
- `count()` and `show(n)` don't have this problem: `count()` returns a single number, and
  `show(n)` only ever prints `n` rows without collecting the rest.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 5 min.** Quiz 6 Q7 tests this risk directly ("main risk of collect() on a very large
DataFrame") — this is a real, industry-relevant footgun, not a trivia fact, so it's worth the full
5 minutes.
:::

---

## Writing DataFrame Output

```python
# Write as CSV — creates a folder, not a single file
df.write.csv("output/path", header=True, mode="overwrite")

# Write as JSON
df.write.json("output/path", mode="overwrite")
```

- `df.write.csv(...)` **is an action** — like `show()` or `count()`, it triggers Spark to execute
  the full pending plan, this time saving the result to storage instead of printing it.
- `mode="overwrite"` replaces existing data at that path; `mode="error"` (the default) fails if
  the path already exists, to prevent accidentally destroying previous output.
- The capstone's `spark_job.py` uses this same write pattern — except writing to MongoDB instead
  of a CSV folder, which Module 5 covers.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** Quiz 6 Q8 and Q9 both test that `write.csv()` is an action, not a
transformation — reinforce that classification explicitly, since "write" sounds like it should
just be setup, not execution.
:::

## Joins in PySpark

```python
# Inner join: only rows with matching keys in both DataFrames
result = ratings.join(movies, on="movieId")

# Left join: all rows from the left DataFrame, matched rows (or nulls) from the right
result = ratings.join(movies, on="movieId", how="left")

# Joining on differently-named columns
result = df1.join(df2, df1["user_id"] == df2["id"])
```

- A **join** combines two DataFrames into one, matching rows where a key column agrees.
- **Inner join** (the default): keep only rows that have a match in *both* DataFrames — rows with
  no match on either side are dropped.
- **Left join:** keep every row from the left DataFrame; unmatched rows get `null` for the right
  DataFrame's columns instead of being dropped.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Think about it
`ratings` has a `movieId` for every rating. `movies` has a `movieId` and `title` for every film.
If you inner-join them, could you ever end up with *fewer* rows than `ratings` had originally?
What would that mean about the data?
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 5 min.** The callout's answer: yes — if some `movieId` in `ratings` has no matching row
in `movies` (a deleted or mislabeled film), the inner join silently drops those ratings. This is
exactly the kind of thing Lab 8's Task 2 depends on getting right.
:::

## Worked Example: A Full Multi-Step Query

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, avg, count, round as spark_round, desc

top_movies = ratings \
    .groupBy("movieId") \
    .agg(spark_round(avg("rating"), 2).alias("avg_rating"),
         count("rating").alias("num_ratings")) \
    .filter(col("num_ratings") >= 50) \
    .join(movies, on="movieId") \
    .select("title", "avg_rating", "num_ratings") \
    .orderBy(desc("avg_rating"))

top_movies.show(10, truncate=False)
```

Reading this top to bottom: group ratings by film, compute each film's average and count, keep
only films with enough ratings to be meaningful, join in the title, keep just the columns we
want, sort by rating, show the top 10.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** This is deliberately close to Lab 8 Task 2's actual solution shape — walk
through it step by step rather than all at once, since chaining six operations together is a lot
to take in as a single block the first time.
:::

## Module 4 Summary

| Concept | Key idea |
|---|---|
| Spark vs. MapReduce | Keeps intermediate data in memory instead of writing to disk every step |
| RDD vs. DataFrame | RDD = unstructured distributed collection; DataFrame = distributed table with a schema |
| SparkSession | One entry point per application; `%%spark` cells already have one built |
| DataFrame | Distributed, schema-aware, and **immutable** — every operation returns a new one |
| Transformation | Lazy — builds a plan (`filter`, `select`, `groupBy`, `join`, ...) |
| Action | Triggers execution (`show`, `count`, `collect`, `write.csv`, ...) |
| `collect()` risk | Pulls all rows to the driver — can crash it on large data |
| Join | Combine two DataFrames on a shared key — inner drops unmatched rows, left keeps them |

**Connects to:** Lab 7, Lab 8, Checkpoints 4 & 5, Quizzes 5 & 6, Final Q16–Q30, Capstone
(`spark_job.py`'s five aggregations)

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** Bridge to Module 5: "Everything computed here has been printed or written to a
CSV so far. Module 5 is about where the *capstone's* output actually goes — a real, shared,
multi-user database — MongoDB."
:::
